notes:
1. Meaning of Political System

A Political System is the framework through which:

  • Political authority is organised.
  • Political power is acquired.
  • Political power is exercised.
  • Political power is transferred.

It determines:

  • How Governments are formed.
  • How laws are made.
  • How policies are implemented.
  • How citizens participate.
  • How power is distributed and controlled.

2. Components of a Political System

The Indian Political System includes:

  • Constitution.
  • Legislature.
  • Executive.
  • Judiciary.
  • Election Commission.
  • Political Parties.
  • Citizens.
  • Public institutions.

3. Objectives of the Political System

The Indian Political System seeks to:

  • Maintain law and order.
  • Protect Fundamental Rights.
  • Promote public welfare.
  • Ensure justice.
  • Provide Good Governance.
  • Maintain national unity.
  • Promote democratic participation.
  • Achieve socio-economic development.

4. Constitutional Foundation

The Indian Political System is founded on the:

  • Constitution of India.

The Constitution came into force on:

  • 26 January 1950.
📌 Must-Memorise

26 January 1950 → Constitution Came into Force

5. Supreme Law

The Constitution is the:

  • Supreme Law of the Land.

All public institutions derive authority from:

  • Constitution.
  • No organ of Government can act beyond constitutional limits.

6. Core Constitutional Features

India's political system is based on:

  • Democracy.
  • Republic.
  • Parliamentary Government.
  • Federalism.
  • Rule of Law.
  • Secularism.
  • Social Justice.
  • Constitutional Supremacy.

7. Democratic System

India is described in the source as:

  • World's Largest Democracy.

Government derives authority from:

  • The People.

Citizens choose representatives through:

  • Periodic elections.

8. Popular Sovereignty

The ultimate source of political power is:

  • The People.

This is reflected in the Preamble:

  • “We, the People of India...”
📌 Must-Memorise

Popular Sovereignty → Power Ultimately Comes from the People

9. Representative Democracy

India follows:

  • Representative Democracy.

Citizens elect representatives who govern:

  • On their behalf.

10. Republic

India is a:

  • Republic.

Its Head of State is:

  • President of India.

The President is:

  • Elected.
  • Not hereditary.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Republic → Elected Head of State Not → Hereditary Monarch

11. Parliamentary Government

India follows:

  • Parliamentary System of Government.

The system is largely borrowed from:

  • United Kingdom.

12. Nominal Executive

At Union level:

  • President is the Constitutional or Nominal Executive.

13. Real Executive

The Real Executive consists of:

  • Prime Minister.
  • Council of Ministers.
📌 Must-Memorise

Nominal Executive → President Real Executive → PM + Council of Ministers

14. Collective Responsibility

The Union Council of Ministers is:

  • Collectively responsible to Lok Sabha.

Constitutional basis:

  • Article 75(3).
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 75(3) → Collective Responsibility to Lok Sabha

15. No-Confidence Motion

If Lok Sabha passes a:

  • No-Confidence Motion,

the entire Council of Ministers must:

  • Resign.

16. Fusion of Executive and Legislature

The parliamentary system involves:

  • Functional overlap between Legislature and Executive.
  • Ministers are generally members of Parliament.
  • Executive remains responsible to Legislature.

17. Opposition

The Opposition plays an important role by:

  • Questioning Government.
  • Examining policies.
  • Protecting public interest.
  • Ensuring accountability.

18. Political Responsibility

The Executive is held accountable through:

  • Question Hour.
  • Zero Hour.
  • Debates.
  • Motions.
  • Parliamentary Committees.

19. Federal Character

India has:

  • Federal System with a Strong Centre.

20. Meaning of Federalism

Federalism means:

Powers are constitutionally divided between:

  • Union Government.
  • State Governments.

Both levels derive authority from:

  • Constitution.

21. Federal Features

The source identifies:

  • Written Constitution.
  • Constitutional Supremacy.
  • Division of Powers.
  • Independent Judiciary.
  • Bicameral Legislature at Union level.
  • Constitutional distribution of authority.

22. Seventh Schedule

Legislative powers are distributed through:

  • Union List.
  • State List.
  • Concurrent List.

These are contained in:

  • Seventh Schedule.
📌 Must-Memorise

Seventh Schedule → Union + State + Concurrent Lists

23. Cooperative Federalism

Cooperative Federalism means:

  • Union and States work together.

Examples identified in the source:

  • GST Council.
  • NITI Aayog.
  • Inter-State Council.

24. Competitive Federalism

Competitive Federalism encourages States to:

  • Improve governance.
  • Attract investment.
  • Improve public services.
  • Promote economic growth.

25. Cooperative vs Competitive Federalism

Cooperative Federalism:

  • Collaboration.

Competitive Federalism:

  • Healthy competition.
  • Both may operate simultaneously within the Indian system.

26. Secular State

India is a:

  • Secular State.

The source states that the State:

  • Has no official religion.
  • Treats religions equally.
  • Protects religious freedom.

27. Constitutional Basis of Secularism

Secularism is reflected through:

  • Preamble.
  • Articles 25–28.
  • Equality provisions.
  • Basic Structure doctrine.

28. Welfare State Objective

The Constitution seeks to establish a:

  • Welfare State.

It aims at:

  • Social justice.
  • Economic justice.
  • Political justice.

29. DPSPs and Welfare State

Directive Principles guide the State toward:

  • Social welfare.
  • Public health.
  • Education.
  • Equality.
  • Economic justice.

30. Voting Age

Every citizen aged:

  • 18 years or above
  • who satisfies legal qualifications may vote.
📌 Must-Memorise

Universal Adult Suffrage → 18 Years

31. Democratic Importance of Adult Suffrage

Universal Adult Suffrage strengthens:

  • Political equality.
  • Representation.
  • Popular sovereignty.
  • Democratic legitimacy.

32. Meaning

Constitutional Government means:

  • Government powers are defined.
  • Government powers are limited.
  • Government powers are controlled by Constitution.

33. Constitutional Supremacy

Every authority including:

  • Parliament.
  • Executive.
  • Judiciary.
  • State Governments

must act according to:

  • Constitution.

34. Meaning

Rule of Law means:

  • No person is above law.
  • Government itself is subject to law.

35. Rule of Law Protects Against

It protects citizens against:

  • Arbitrary Government action.
  • Abuse of authority.
  • Discrimination.
  • Illegal detention.
  • Unfair administrative decisions.

36. Three Organs

Governmental power is distributed among:

  • Legislature.
  • Executive.
  • Judiciary.

37. Indian Position

India does not follow:

  • Rigid Separation of Powers.

It follows:

  • Functional Separation.
  • Coordination.
  • Mutual accountability.
  • Constitutional limitations.
📌 Must-Memorise

India → Functional Separation, Not Rigid Separation

38. Legislature

The Legislature:

  • Makes laws.
  • Controls finances.
  • Represents people.
  • Holds Executive accountable.

39. Executive

The Executive:

  • Implements laws.
  • Administers Government.
  • Maintains public order.
  • Formulates policies.

40. Judiciary

The Judiciary:

  • Interprets laws.
  • Protects Constitution.
  • Protects Fundamental Rights.
  • Resolves disputes.
  • Exercises Judicial Review.

41. Meaning

Checks and Balances ensure that:

  • No organ becomes all-powerful.
  • Each organ is subject to constitutional controls.

42. Legislature Checks Executive

Parliament exercises control through:

  • Question Hour.
  • No-Confidence Motion.
  • Budget approval.
  • Committees.
  • Debates.

43. Executive Checks Legislature

The Executive may:

  • Recommend legislation.
  • Summon Parliament.
  • Prorogue Parliament.
  • Advise dissolution of Lok Sabha.
  • Use Ordinance power through President under Article 123 subject to constitutional conditions.

44. Judiciary Checks Legislature

Judiciary may:

  • Exercise Judicial Review.
  • Strike down unconstitutional laws.
  • Protect Fundamental Rights.

45. Judiciary Checks Executive

Judiciary may:

  • Review executive actions.
  • Issue writs.
  • Prevent abuse of power.

46. Parliament

At Union level, Parliament consists of:

  • President.
  • Rajya Sabha.
  • Lok Sabha.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 79 → President + Rajya Sabha + Lok Sabha

47. State Legislature

At State level, Legislature consists of:

  • Governor.
  • One or two Houses depending on State.

48. Legislative Functions

The Legislature:

  • Debates laws.
  • Enacts laws.
  • Represents citizens.
  • Controls finance.
  • Holds Executive accountable.
  • Participates in constitutional amendment where required.

49. Legislative Competence

Parliament can legislate on:

  • Union List.
  • Concurrent List.
  • State List in constitutionally permitted circumstances.

State Legislatures mainly legislate on:

  • State List.
  • Concurrent List.

50. Financial Control

Legislature controls public finance through:

  • Budget.
  • Demands for Grants.
  • Appropriation Bills.
  • Finance Bills.
  • Audit scrutiny.
  • Financial Committees.

51. Constitutional Amendment

Parliament may amend Constitution under:

  • Article 368.

Specified amendments also require ratification by:

  • At least half of State Legislatures.

52. Union Executive

Union Executive includes:

  • President.
  • Vice-President.
  • Prime Minister.
  • Council of Ministers.
  • Civil Services.

53. State Executive

State Executive includes:

  • Governor.
  • Chief Minister.
  • Council of Ministers.
  • State administration.

54. Policy Formulation

The political Executive formulates policies relating to:

  • Economic development.
  • National security.
  • Foreign affairs.
  • Public welfare.
  • Social justice.
  • Administration.

55. Implementation

The Executive:

  • Implements laws.
  • Maintains public order.
  • Collects revenue.
  • Administers welfare schemes.
  • Executes development programmes.

56. Executive's Legislative Role

The Executive also participates in:

  • Introducing Bills.
  • Recommending Money Bills.
  • Delegated legislation.
  • Ordinances.
  • Summoning and proroguing Legislatures.

57. Emergency Role

The Executive plays an important role during:

  • National emergencies.
  • Constitutional emergencies.
  • Financial emergencies.
  • Natural disasters.
  • Security crises.

Its actions remain subject to:

  • Constitution.
  • Judicial Review.

58. Integrated Judicial System

India has an integrated Judiciary consisting of:

  • Supreme Court.
  • High Courts.
  • Subordinate Courts.

59. Constitutional Interpretation

Judiciary interprets:

  • Constitution.
  • Statutes.
  • Rights and duties.
  • Distribution of powers.

60. Judicial Review

Judicial Review allows courts to test validity of:

  • Laws.
  • Executive actions.
  • Constitutional amendments subject to Basic Structure doctrine.

61. Article 32

Article 32 empowers:

  • Supreme Court

to enforce:

  • Fundamental Rights.

62. Article 226

Article 226 empowers:

  • High Courts

to issue writs for:

  • Fundamental Rights.
  • Other legal rights.

63. Article 131

Supreme Court has Original Jurisdiction in certain disputes involving:

  • Union and States.
  • States among themselves.

64. Judicial Independence

Judicial independence is protected through:

  • Security of tenure.
  • Fixed service conditions.
  • Difficult removal procedure.
  • Separation from Executive.
  • Contempt powers.
  • Constitutional status.

81. Meaning

Good Governance means administration that is:

  • Transparent.
  • Accountable.
  • Responsive.
  • Efficient.
  • Inclusive.
  • Governed by law.

The source identifies:

  • Rule of Law.
  • Transparency.
  • Accountability.
  • Participation.
  • Responsiveness.
  • Efficiency.
  • Effectiveness.
  • Equity.
  • Inclusiveness.
  • Consensus-oriented decision-making.

83. Meaning

Accountability means:

  • Public authorities must explain and justify decisions.
  • They must accept responsibility for actions.

84. Political Accountability

The Council of Ministers remains accountable to:

  • Elected Legislature.

85. Legislative Accountability

The Legislature holds Executive accountable through:

  • Questions.
  • Debates.
  • Motions.
  • Financial control.
  • Committees.

86. Judicial Accountability of Government

Executive and legislative actions remain subject to:

  • Judicial Review

when they violate:

  • Constitution.
  • Law.

87. Administrative Accountability

Civil servants remain accountable through:

  • Service rules.
  • Departmental supervision.
  • Vigilance mechanisms.
  • Audits.
  • Disciplinary proceedings.

88. Financial Accountability

Financial accountability operates through:

  • Budget approval.
  • Legislative control.
  • CAG audit.
  • Financial Committees.

89. Public Accountability

Citizens hold Government accountable through:

  • Elections.
  • Public consultation.
  • Media scrutiny.
  • Social audits.
  • Grievance mechanisms.
  • Right to Information.

90. Meaning

Transparency means:

  • Openness in Government functioning.
  • Public access to relevant information.

91. Mechanisms Promoting Transparency

The source identifies:

  • RTI.
  • Proactive disclosure.
  • E-Governance.
  • Open budgeting.
  • Audit reports.
  • Transparent procurement.

  • Decision-making.
  • Implementation.
  • Evaluation.

Representative Democracy:

  • Citizens elect representatives.

Participatory Democracy:

  • Citizens participate directly in governance processes.

95. Role of Media

An independent and responsible media:

  • Informs citizens.
  • Investigates issues.
  • Exposes wrongdoing.
  • Encourages debate.
  • Strengthens accountability.

96. Role of Civil Society

Civil society contributes through:

  • Awareness.
  • Research.
  • Monitoring.
  • Advocacy.
  • Assistance to vulnerable groups.
  • Policy reform.

97. E-Governance

E-Governance is the use of:

  • Information and Communication Technology

in:

  • Administration.
  • Public-service delivery.

98. Benefits of E-Governance

It may:

  • Reduce delays.
  • Simplify procedures.
  • Create digital records.
  • Increase traceability.
  • Expand access.
  • Reduce unnecessary personal interaction.

99. Safeguards for E-Governance

Technology must be supported by:

  • Cybersecurity.
  • Privacy protection.
  • Inclusive access.

100. Grievance Redressal

A grievance system allows complaints relating to:

  • Delay.
  • Denial of benefits.
  • Negligence.
  • Misconduct.
  • Corruption.
  • Unfair treatment.

101. Social Audit

Social Audit enables citizens to examine:

  • Beneficiary lists.
  • Expenditure records.
  • Public works.
  • Service quality.
  • Scheme compliance.

102. Criminalisation of Politics

The participation of persons facing serious criminal allegations may weaken:

  • Institutional credibility.
  • Public confidence.

103. Responses to Criminalisation

The source identifies:

  • Candidate disclosure.
  • Timely trials.
  • Informed voting.

104. Money Power in Elections

High campaign expenditure and opaque funding may:

  • Distort electoral competition.
  • Increase influence of wealthy donors.

105. Corruption

Corruption:

  • Weakens institutions.
  • Diverts public resources.
  • Reduces trust.

106. Defections

Political defections may:

  • Alter electoral mandates.
  • Destabilise Governments.

107. Anti-Defection Limitation

A continuing concern is:

  • Delay in deciding disqualification petitions.

108. Weak Inner-Party Democracy

Concentrated authority within political parties may weaken:

  • Internal elections.
  • Leadership competition.
  • Member participation.

109. Social and Economic Inequality

Unequal access to:

  • Education.
  • Healthcare.
  • Employment.
  • Political influence
  • may weaken substantive democracy.

110. Identity-Based Polarisation

Political mobilisation based excessively on:

  • Caste.
  • Religion.
  • Language.
  • Region
  • may deepen social division.

111. Misinformation

False or manipulated digital content can:

  • Distort public debate.
  • Distort electoral choice.

112. Institutional Conflict

Disputes may arise over:

  • Jurisdiction.
  • Appointments.
  • Legislation.
  • Administrative authority.

Such disputes should be resolved through:

  • Constitutional processes.
  • Dialogue.
  • Judicial interpretation where required.

113. Centre–State Tensions

  • Legislative competence.
  • Financial distribution.
  • Governor's powers.
  • Central agencies.
  • Inter-State resources.

114. Delay in Justice

Judicial delay may weaken:

  • Enforcement of rights.
  • Public confidence.

  • Judicial reform.
  • Better infrastructure.
  • ADR.
  • Efficient procedures.

115. Administrative Capacity

Government institutions may face:

  • Staff shortages.
  • Training gaps.
  • Technology gaps.
  • Resource limitations.

The source recommends:

  • Transparent political funding.
  • Electoral reforms.
  • Judicial reforms.
  • Stronger legislative scrutiny.
  • Independent constitutional institutions.

175. Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, 1978

The Supreme Court held Article 21 procedure must be:

  • Just.
  • Fair.
  • Reasonable.

Maneka Gandhi linked:

  • Article 14.
  • Article 19.
  • Article 21.

177. Minerva Mills v. Union of India, 1980

The Supreme Court held:

  • Limited amending power is Basic Structure.
  • Harmony between Fundamental Rights and DPSPs is part of constitutional structure.

178. Waman Rao v. Union of India, 1981

The Supreme Court distinguished Ninth Schedule laws inserted:

  • Before 24 April 1973.
  • After 24 April 1973.

The Supreme Court held:

  • Politically subjective dismissal of State Governments is impermissible.

211. Political System vs Government

Political System:

  • Complete and continuing framework.
  • Includes Constitution, institutions and citizens.

Government:

  • Temporary governing authority.
  • Changes after elections.

212. Democracy vs Republic

Democracy:

  • Government based on people's participation.

Republic:

  • Head of State is elected.
  • No hereditary ruler.

213. Parliamentary vs Presidential System

Parliamentary:

  • Executive responsible to Legislature.
  • PM is Real Executive.
  • Collective Responsibility.

Presidential:

  • Executive independent of Legislature.
  • President is Real Executive.
  • Fixed tenure.

214. Federal vs Unitary

Federal:

  • Constitutional division of powers.

Unitary:

  • Centralised authority.

India:

  • Federal with a strong Centre.

215. Separation of Powers vs Checks and Balances

Separation:

  • Distribution of functions.

Checks and Balances:

  • Mutual constitutional control.

216. Good Governance vs E-Governance

Good Governance:

  • Broad principle of accountable and effective administration.

E-Governance:

  • Technology-based administrative tool.

217. Transparency vs Accountability

Transparency:

  • Makes Government visible.

Accountability:

  • Makes Government answerable.
